paras.A: For most of history, reading was a slow and deliberate activity. Books were rare and expensive, and a reader who owned only a handful of them would return to the same pages many times. The spread of printing, and later of newspapers and the internet, changed that pattern completely. Today the average educated adult encounters thousands of words every day, most of them on a screen, and the dominant skill is no longer careful reading but rapid scanning.
paras.B: Scanning is, of course, a useful skill. Nobody wants to read every line of a timetable or a set of instructions. The difficulty arises when the habit spreads to texts that deserve more attention. Researchers who track eye movements have found that readers of online articles tend to follow an F-shaped pattern: they read the first lines, skim down the left margin and miss much of what lies in between. Even highly experienced readers can find themselves doing this with material that they intend to study.
paras.C: The consequences are not merely a matter of missing details. A series of experiments in Norway asked two groups of students to read the same short story, one on paper and one on a tablet. Both groups said they enjoyed it equally, but the paper readers were noticeably better at placing events in order. The researchers suggested that a printed book offers physical clues, such as the thickness of the pages already read, that help the brain to construct a mental map of the plot. Critics point out that the sample was small and that younger participants, who grew up with tablets, might perform differently.
paras.D: Defenders of digital reading argue that the format is not the real issue; attention is. A reader who switches between a novel and a messaging application every few minutes will remember little on any medium. Some educators have therefore begun to teach 'deep reading' as a deliberate skill. Students are asked to read a short passage without interruption, write a summary from memory and then compare it with the original. Teachers report that the exercise is uncomfortable at first, because many pupils have rarely spent twenty minutes on a single text, but that most improve within weeks.
paras.E: Differences between languages complicate the debate. Readers of Chinese, which uses thousands of separate characters, appear to rely more on visual memory than readers of Spanish, whose spelling closely follows pronunciation. A study comparing the two groups found that both slowed down when the text became difficult, but they did so in different places. This suggests that the 'right' speed for reading is not a universal quantity, and that advice given in one country may transfer poorly to another.
paras.F: Age is a further factor. Older readers, who learned to read before screens became common, often say that they find it hard to concentrate on a monitor, whereas many teenagers insist that they prefer it. Psychologists urge caution here. People tend to remember their own preferences more accurately than their results, and in several tests the readers who felt most comfortable with a medium were not the ones who understood the most. Comfort, in other words, is a poor guide to performance.
paras.G: There is also a social dimension. Slow readers tend to engage with an argument rather than a conclusion: they notice assumptions, test evidence and, occasionally, change their minds. In a media environment designed to reward immediate reactions, this patience has become unusual, and some commentators regard it as a civic virtue rather than a personal preference. Whether or not that claim is exaggerated, it highlights something that rapid scanning cannot supply, namely the chance to think while reading rather than after it.
paras.H: None of this requires abandoning technology. Libraries now lend electronic books, and e-readers with simple screens avoid many of the distractions of a tablet. The practical recommendation that emerges from the research is modest: choose the method to fit the purpose. Scan the timetable, skim the news, but give the difficult book your full attention, preferably in a quiet place and without a phone nearby.

paras.A: In an age of abundant information, the scarce resource is no longer facts but the attention needed to absorb them. The economist Herbert Simon observed as early as 1971 that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. His remark has become more relevant with every passing decade, as screens, notifications and endless streams of content compete for the few hours in which people are awake and alert.
paras.B: Many digital services are offered free of charge, but they are not truly free. Their income comes from advertisers who pay to place messages in front of users, and the time that users spend is therefore the product being sold. This arrangement gives companies a strong reason to design services that hold attention for as long as possible, using bright colours, automatic video playback and rewards that arrive at unpredictable moments.
paras.C: Psychologists have long known that unpredictable rewards are especially compelling. A gambler pulling the lever of a machine never knows when a win will come, and the uncertainty keeps the habit alive. Checking a phone has a similar structure: most of the time there is nothing of interest, but occasionally there is a message or a surprising image, and that occasional reward is enough to encourage repeated checking throughout the day.
paras.D: The costs to individuals are difficult to measure but appear to be real. Experiments show that even the presence of a phone on a desk, switched off, can slightly reduce performance on tasks that demand concentration. Workers who are interrupted need many minutes to return to the original task, and some studies suggest that people who switch constantly between activities complete fewer of them than those who do one thing at a time.
paras.E: Society as a whole may also pay a price. When attention is directed towards whatever is most emotional or surprising, careful discussion of complicated matters struggles to compete. Critics argue that this encourages extreme opinions, because moderate views rarely attract the same interest. Defenders of the platforms reply that people are free to choose what they watch, and that new forms of expression have also given a voice to many who were previously ignored.
paras.F: Responses are emerging at several levels. Some individuals use apps that limit their screen time, while a few schools have banned phones from classrooms and report better results in lessons. Regulators in several countries are considering rules that would require platforms to switch off the most addictive features for children. Whether such measures succeed will depend on whether attention is eventually recognised as something worth protecting.
paras.G: Some thinkers propose a more positive vision. If attention is scarce, they argue, then the most valuable skill of the future will be the ability to direct it deliberately. Practices such as reading for long periods without interruption, keeping the phone in another room and scheduling time for deep work have attracted new followers, and several companies now measure the 'focus hours' of their staff. What was once taken for granted, the capacity to concentrate, is increasingly treated as something that has to be trained.

paras.A: Biodiversity, the variety of living things on Earth, is usually discussed in terms of species, but it also includes the genetic differences within a species and the range of habitats in which they live. Scientists have so far described about two million species, yet estimates of the real total range from five million to far more than that, since insects, fungi and deep-sea creatures are still poorly known.
paras.B: Extinction is a natural process. Over the history of life, more than ninety-nine per cent of all species that ever existed have disappeared. On five occasions, however, extinction rates rose so sharply that a majority of species vanished within a short period of geological time. The best known of these events, about sixty-six million years ago, ended the reign of the dinosaurs, probably following the impact of a large asteroid.
paras.C: Many biologists now argue that a sixth mass extinction is under way, and that this time humans are responsible. Current rates of loss are thought to be tens or hundreds of times higher than the natural background rate. The main causes are the destruction of habitats for farming and building, overhunting and overfishing, the spread of invasive species, pollution and, increasingly, climate change.
paras.D: Why should this matter, beyond the sadness of losing beautiful animals? One answer is practical. Ecosystems provide services on which people depend, such as the pollination of crops, the purification of water and the protection of coasts by mangroves and reefs. Many medicines were first discovered in plants and fungi, and each lost species is a library of chemical ideas that can never be read.
paras.E: A second answer is ethical. Some philosophers argue that other species have a value of their own, regardless of whether they are useful to us. Others emphasise our responsibility to future generations, who will inherit a poorer world if the present trend continues. These two positions lead to different arguments, but they often arrive at the same practical conclusion.
paras.F: There are reasons for cautious hope. Protected areas now cover a growing portion of land and sea, and well-managed projects have rescued species from the brink, such as the California condor and the Arabian oryx. Success, however, depends on money, on cooperation between nations and on addressing the pressures that cause losses in the first place. Protection of single species, without protection of their habitats, is unlikely to be enough.
paras.G: Individuals can contribute, too. Choosing food and wood products from sustainable sources, avoiding the release of pets and garden plants into the wild, and supporting local conservation groups all make a modest difference when many people do them. Citizen science projects, in which volunteers record birds, insects and plants with their phones, now provide scientists with data on a scale that no professional team could collect, and they help to build public concern for nature. Over time, such small actions can also influence companies and governments, which respond when enough citizens show that they care.

paras.A: Since the discovery of the structure of DNA in 1953, scientists have gradually learned to read and change the instructions that guide living things. Genetic engineering, the deliberate alteration of an organism's genes, was once a laboratory curiosity. Today it is used to produce medicines, to improve crops and, in some experiments, to correct inherited diseases in human cells.
paras.B: In agriculture, the technology has produced plants that resist insects, tolerate drought or contain extra vitamins. Supporters claim that such crops can raise yields and reduce the use of chemical sprays, helping to feed a growing population. Opponents respond that the long-term effects on the environment are uncertain, and that a few large companies control the seeds, leaving farmers dependent on them.
paras.C: Medicine has seen more rapid acceptance. Insulin for diabetes, once extracted from animals, is now made by bacteria that carry a human gene. More recently, a technique known as CRISPR has made it much easier and cheaper to edit genes precisely. Early trials have treated some blood disorders, and researchers hope that other conditions caused by a single faulty gene may eventually be cured.
paras.D: The most controversial question concerns changes to human embryos. Alterations in ordinary body cells affect only the patient, but alterations in embryos would be inherited by all later generations. In 2018, a scientist in China announced that he had created babies with edited genes. The announcement was widely condemned, and he was later imprisoned, because the safety of the procedure had not been established and consent could not be obtained from those affected.
paras.E: Philosophers disagree about where to draw the line. Some argue that treating serious disease is morally acceptable, but 'enhancement', such as choosing a child's height or intelligence, is not. Others reply that the distinction is hard to maintain, since many treatments, like vaccines, already improve on nature. There is also the concern that costly technology could widen the gap between rich and poor.
paras.F: Most countries therefore regulate the field closely. Public discussion is important, since decisions about the human genome concern everyone, not only scientists. Many experts suggest that rules should be flexible enough to allow beneficial research but firm enough to prevent abuse, and that they should be agreed internationally, so that dangerous experiments cannot simply move to places with fewer controls.
paras.G: Public opinion about these questions varies widely from country to country. Surveys show greater acceptance of genetic treatments for disease than of altered food, which is the reverse of what many scientists expect, since the evidence for the safety of approved crops is considerable. Experts suggest that distrust often grows when people feel that decisions were made without them, and that clear explanation and open debate are as important as the technology itself. Trust, once lost, is hard to rebuild, and a single scandal can set back years of careful and honest research.

paras.A: In 1950, fewer than a third of the world's people lived in cities. Today the figure is more than half, and the United Nations expects it to reach about two-thirds by the middle of this century. Most of the growth is taking place in Asia and Africa, where cities such as Lagos, Dhaka and Kinshasa are adding hundreds of thousands of inhabitants every year.
paras.B: People move to cities for good reasons. Wages are generally higher, schools and hospitals are closer and the range of jobs is wider. Economists note that no country has become wealthy without large-scale urbanisation, since concentrating people allows firms to share suppliers, workers to find specialised jobs and ideas to spread. In this sense, cities are engines of growth.
paras.C: Yet rapid growth often outpaces the ability of authorities to provide services. Roughly one billion people live in informal settlements, where houses are built without permission on land they do not own, and water, sewers and electricity may be lacking. Residents of these areas face disease, fire and the constant fear of eviction, though many show remarkable ingenuity in organising their own neighbourhoods.
paras.D: Transport is another challenge. In cities built for walking, a rapid increase in cars leads to congestion and polluted air, and the time wasted in traffic reduces productivity. Some cities have responded by building bus lanes, cable cars or underground railways. Medellín in Colombia, for example, linked poor hillside districts to the centre by cable cars, which shortened journeys dramatically.
paras.E: Environmental problems also deserve attention. Dense cities can be efficient, since people living in apartments use less energy per head than those in scattered houses, but they also concentrate waste and pollution. Cities built on flat coastal land are exposed to rising seas and storms, and the poorest residents, living in the most vulnerable areas, are usually the first to suffer.
paras.F: Planners increasingly agree that the aim should not be to stop migration but to prepare for it. Investment in basic services, secure land rights for residents and public transport before demand becomes overwhelming can make growth manageable. Cities that plan ahead have the opportunity to avoid the mistakes of those that grew earlier, and to become healthier, fairer places in which to live.
paras.G: Smaller cities deserve attention, too. Much of the discussion focuses on giant capitals, yet a large share of the growth is happening in towns of fewer than a million people, where planning offices are small and funds are limited. Helping these towns to prepare for growth, with good roads, clean water and land records, may prove cheaper and more effective than trying to repair the problems of the giants after the damage has been done. International lenders and aid agencies could play a larger role by directing a fairer share of their support towards such towns and the people who live in them.

paras.A: Writing is one of humanity's most important inventions, yet it is surprisingly recent. Speech has existed for tens of thousands of years, at least, but the earliest known writing dates from only about five thousand years ago. It appeared independently in several places, most notably in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Central America, which suggests that it arises naturally once societies become complex enough.
paras.B: The earliest writing was not literature but bookkeeping. In the Sumerian city of Uruk, in what is now Iraq, officials pressed marks into wet clay to record quantities of grain, sheep and beer. Early signs were simple pictures, but over time they became more abstract, and scribes began to use wedge-shaped strokes made with a reed, a style now called cuneiform.
paras.C: A crucial step was the discovery that signs could represent sounds rather than objects. Once a picture of a bee, say, could stand for the sound 'be', scribes could spell out names and abstract ideas that are hard to draw. Combining sound signs with picture signs produced flexible systems such as Egyptian hieroglyphs, which could record anything from tax lists to religious poetry.
paras.D: The alphabet was a further simplification. Instead of hundreds of signs, it uses a small set of letters, each standing for a single sound. The earliest alphabets developed around 1800 BC among Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt, and the Phoenicians later spread a version across the Mediterranean. The Greeks added letters for vowels, and from their script come both the Latin and the Cyrillic alphabets.
paras.E: The consequences of writing were far-reaching. Laws could be recorded and applied consistently, and rulers could administer larger territories. Knowledge could survive its author, so that later generations could build on earlier discoveries rather than rediscover them. Some thinkers, however, feared the change: Socrates, as reported by his pupil Plato, argued that written words would weaken memory.
paras.F: Today, writing is changing again. Many people write more than ever, in messages and posts, but their style is often closer to speech. Some linguists see this as a return to the origins of language, while others worry that careful, extended writing is becoming rarer. Whatever happens, the story of writing shows how a practical tool for counting grain became the foundation of civilisation.
paras.G: Writing also changed how people thought about time and authority. Once a promise or a debt was written down, it could be checked years later, and disagreements could be settled by consulting the tablet rather than by trusting a witness. Scribes became a powerful class because they alone could read and write, and in many societies, learning to do so remained a privilege of the few for centuries, until printing and public schools opened literacy to ordinary people. Even today, the ability to read and write remains one of the clearest dividing lines between opportunity and disadvantage in many parts of the world.

paras.A: Medicine generates more information than any doctor can follow. Every year, thousands of studies appear, and each patient produces scans, test results and notes. Computer programs that learn from large collections of data, usually described as artificial intelligence, are increasingly used to help doctors find the important facts and make better decisions.
paras.B: One successful area is the reading of images. Programs trained on hundreds of thousands of X-rays, skin photographs and eye scans can learn to spot signs of disease, sometimes as accurately as specialists. In busy hospitals, such a program can sort scans so that urgent cases are examined first, and in places with few specialists, it can offer a second opinion that would otherwise not exist.
paras.C: Another application is the discovery of new drugs. Developing a medicine usually takes more than ten years and costs billions of dollars, because thousands of chemical candidates must be tested. Programs can predict which molecules are likely to work, allowing researchers to concentrate on the most promising ones. In 2020, a system predicted the shapes of proteins with remarkable accuracy, a problem that biologists had struggled with for fifty years.
paras.D: The technology has important limits. A program is only as good as the data it learned from, and if the training examples came mainly from one group of people, it may perform badly on others. Some systems have also proved difficult to explain: they give an answer, but not the reason, and a doctor who cannot understand the reasoning may find it hard to trust the result.
paras.E: Questions of responsibility are unresolved. If a program misses a cancer, who is to blame: the doctor, the hospital or the company that wrote the software? Most experts insist that the final decision must remain with a human professional, and that programs should be treated as assistants. Patients, too, have the right to know when software has influenced their care.
paras.F: Privacy is a further concern. Medical records are among the most personal information that exists, and large collections of them attract criminals as well as researchers. Careful rules about who may see the data, and about removing names from records, are necessary if the public is to support the use of health data for research.
paras.G: Despite these concerns, many doctors are optimistic. They hope that by handling routine tasks such as paperwork and the first sorting of scans, the technology will free them to spend more time with patients. If that happens, the most human parts of medicine, listening and explaining, may become more important rather than less.

paras.A: When patients are given a pill that contains no active ingredient but are told it is a powerful medicine, many report that they feel better. This is known as the placebo effect, from the Latin for 'I shall please'. Far from being an imaginary result, it produces measurable changes, and it has become an important subject of study for both doctors and psychologists.
paras.B: The effect has been recognised for a long time, but the first large investigations occurred during the Second World War, when an American doctor ran short of morphine and injected wounded soldiers with salt water instead. To his surprise, many soldiers experienced relief from pain. Since then, trials of new medicines have routinely included a group that receives a placebo, so that the real effect of the drug can be separated from the effect of expectation.
paras.C: Research suggests that placebos work by changing the way the brain handles symptoms. Brain scans show that when people expect pain relief, regions involved in pain are less active, and the body can release its own natural painkillers. The effect is strongest for conditions that depend on perception, such as pain, nausea, tiredness and low mood, and is weaker for illnesses such as infections or broken bones.
paras.D: The way a placebo is given influences its power. Larger pills seem to work better than small ones, injections better than tablets, and expensive-looking packaging better than plain. A warm, confident doctor increases the effect. Surprisingly, there is some evidence that placebos can help even when patients are told honestly that the pill is a placebo, which suggests that the ritual of treatment itself matters.
paras.E: Placebos raise ethical problems. Is it right for a doctor to deceive a patient, even for the patient's benefit? Most medical organisations say no, because trust is the basis of medicine and a deception, once discovered, can damage it. Some doctors argue for a compromise in which they openly explain that a harmless treatment may help through the body's own mechanisms.
paras.F: There is also a reverse effect, called the nocebo effect. People who are warned that a medicine may cause headaches or sickness sometimes experience those symptoms even when given a placebo. This has led to careful discussion of how side effects should be explained, so that patients are properly informed but not made unnecessarily afraid.
paras.G: The placebo effect does not mean that illness is 'all in the mind'. Rather, it shows how closely mind and body are connected, and how much the experience of care contributes to recovery. For researchers, it is a reminder that every treatment, however scientific, takes place in a human relationship.

paras.A: Famous historic places attract millions of visitors each year. Tourism brings income, jobs and a feeling of pride to local people, and it can pay for the preservation of buildings that might otherwise fall into ruin. Yet the same crowds can damage the places they come to admire, creating a dilemma for those responsible for protecting cultural heritage.
paras.B: The physical damage is easy to see. Millions of footsteps wear away ancient stones, the breath and sweat of visitors raise humidity in closed tombs and caves, and touching leaves oil on painted surfaces. The famous caves at Lascaux in France, decorated by prehistoric artists, were closed to the public in 1963 after algae and fungi began to spread over the paintings; today, visitors see an accurate copy nearby.
paras.C: There is also a cultural cost. In some towns, local shops have been replaced by souvenir stands and restaurants aimed at foreigners, and rents have risen so that residents can no longer afford to live there. Venice, with a population that has fallen sharply in recent decades, is often cited as an example of a city in danger of becoming a museum rather than a community.
paras.D: Managers have tried various solutions. Some sites limit the number of visitors per day and require tickets to be booked in advance. Others raise prices at busy times, spread attention to less famous places, or close areas for rest, as is done in some national parks. A few cities now charge day visitors an entry fee, using the money to pay for cleaning and repair.
paras.E: Technology offers further options. Detailed digital models allow people to explore fragile places from home, and virtual reality can recreate sites that have been destroyed. Supporters believe that such tools can bring knowledge to people who could never travel, while critics note that a screen cannot replace the experience of standing in a real place.
paras.F: Local communities should have a voice. Experts point out that heritage is not only a collection of old buildings but a living tradition of festivals, crafts and skills. paras.A: A generation ago, most people expected to work for a single employer, often for a lifetime. Today, millions earn their living by taking short jobs arranged through websites and apps: driving passengers, delivering food, translating documents or designing logos. This pattern of work, in which people are paid for individual tasks rather than a regular salary, is often called the 'gig economy'.
paras.B: For workers, the attraction is flexibility. A student can drive in the evenings, a parent can work during school hours, and someone with a regular job can earn extra money at weekends. For people who find it hard to get a traditional job, because of where they live or because they lack experience, the apps offer an opening that might not otherwise exist.
paras.C: For customers and companies, the advantages are speed and price. A taxi can arrive within minutes, and a business can hire a designer for a single project without the long-term cost of a permanent employee. Platforms also make it easy to compare prices and read ratings by previous customers, which reduces the risk of choosing a poor provider.
paras.D: However, the system has weaknesses. Most gig workers are classed as independent contractors, not employees, and therefore do not receive sick pay, paid holidays or a pension. Income can change from week to week, and when demand is low, a worker may spend hours waiting for jobs. Some surveys suggest that, after the cost of fuel and vehicle repairs, earnings can fall below the minimum wage.
paras.E: Workers also have little say in how they are managed. A rating system allows customers to judge them, and a few poor scores can mean loss of access to the platform, often with no explanation. Because the 'boss' is an algorithm, there is nobody to talk to when something goes wrong. Campaigners argue that this gives companies power without the usual duties of an employer.
paras.F: Governments are responding in different ways. Courts in several countries have ruled that certain drivers should be treated as employees, while some regions have introduced special rules guaranteeing a minimum payment per hour. Companies warn that stricter rules may raise prices and reduce flexibility, but they have also begun to offer limited insurance schemes.
paras.G: The gig economy is unlikely to disappear. Instead, the challenge is to find a balance that keeps the flexibility many workers value while protecting them from the greatest risks. How that balance is struck will help to decide whether the new patterns of work are a chance for progress or a return to insecure employment.

paras.A: The level of the sea has been rising for more than a century, at first slowly and now faster. The main causes are the melting of glaciers and ice sheets and the expansion of water as it warms. Since 1900, the global average has risen by roughly twenty centimetres, and projections for the end of this century range from a few tens of centimetres to more than a metre, depending on future emissions.
paras.B: These figures may sound modest, but their effects are magnified by storms. A higher base level means that storm surges reach farther inland, and coastal floods that once occurred every century may happen every few years. Salt water can also seep into groundwater and farmland, making drinking water unusable and reducing harvests in low-lying river deltas.
paras.C: A large share of the world's population lives near the coast. Cities such as Jakarta, Miami, Shanghai and Alexandria are exposed, and in some of them the land is sinking because water has been pumped from the ground, which makes matters worse. Jakarta is sinking so fast that the government of Indonesia has decided to build a new capital elsewhere.
paras.D: Engineers have long experience of defending coasts. The Netherlands, a third of which lies below sea level, has built dykes, barriers and pumping stations over many centuries. London is protected by a movable barrier across the Thames. Such defences are expensive, however, and not every country has the resources, so poor regions face a greater danger.
paras.E: Alternatives to concrete walls are attracting interest. Wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs absorb the energy of waves, and restoring them can be cheaper and provide homes for wildlife. Some cities are creating parks that flood on purpose, giving water room to spread, while new buildings are raised on supports so that the ground floor can be flooded without serious damage.
paras.F: For some communities, the best option may be to move. Planned retreat is politically difficult, because it means abandoning homes and places of memory, and the people affected must be treated fairly. Several island nations in the Pacific are already thinking about where their citizens might live in the future, and what will happen to their culture.
paras.G: The measures taken during the next few decades will matter greatly. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions will limit how much the sea rises, while good planning will determine how well people cope with the rise that cannot be avoided. Waiting for certainty is not a safe strategy, because the cost of acting late is far greater than the cost of acting early.

paras.A: Nuclear power stations produce electricity by splitting atoms of uranium, which releases heat to boil water and drive turbines. About ten per cent of the world's electricity comes from this source. Because the process burns no fuel in the usual sense, nuclear plants emit almost no carbon dioxide while operating, which has led some environmentalists to reconsider an energy source they once opposed.
paras.B: The advantages are significant. A small amount of uranium contains enormous energy: one kilogram can produce as much electricity as thousands of kilograms of coal. A nuclear plant runs day and night regardless of weather, supplying a steady base of power that wind and solar energy, which vary, cannot provide on their own. France obtains roughly two-thirds of its electricity from nuclear plants and has some of the cleanest electricity in Europe.
paras.C: The disadvantages are equally real. Accidents at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 showed that, although rare, failures can have terrible and long-lasting consequences, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to leave their homes. Statistics suggest that nuclear power causes fewer deaths per unit of energy than coal, but the fear of accidents is strong, and fear has political effects.
paras.D: Waste is another issue. Spent fuel stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years and must be isolated from people and water. Most countries store it in temporary sites while debating permanent solutions, such as burial deep underground. Finland is building the first such repository, but many others have found it hard to persuade local communities to accept one.
paras.E: Cost is perhaps the largest obstacle in practice. New plants have often taken far longer and cost far more than planned, partly because of strict safety demands. Meanwhile, the price of solar and wind power has fallen dramatically. Critics argue that money spent on nuclear projects would reduce emissions faster if invested in renewable energy and storage.
paras.F: Supporters respond that the world cannot afford to ignore any low-carbon source. They point to new designs, such as small modular reactors built in factories, which could be cheaper and safer, and to research on fusion, which joins atoms instead of splitting them and would produce little long-lived waste. Fusion, however, has been 'thirty years away' for decades.
paras.G: The debate is unlikely to end soon. Countries differ in their geography, resources and history, so it is natural that their choices differ. What seems certain is that the decision should be based on evidence of costs, risks and benefits, rather than on slogans from either side.

paras.A: People like to think of themselves as rational decision-makers who weigh the evidence and choose the best option. Psychologists have shown, however, that human judgement is often guided by mental shortcuts. These shortcuts, called heuristics, are usually quick and useful, but they can also lead to systematic mistakes, which researchers call biases.
paras.B: The psychologist Daniel Kahneman described two modes of thinking. The first is fast, automatic and intuitive; it recognises a friend's face or reacts to danger without effort. The second is slow, careful and logical; it is used to solve a mathematical problem or compare two job offers. Most daily decisions are made by the first system, and the second, which requires effort, is used only when necessary.
paras.C: One well-known bias is anchoring. If people are first shown a high number, even a random one, their later estimates tend to be higher than if they had seen a low number. Sellers use this effect when they display a high 'original' price next to a reduced one, making the discount seem larger. Even experts, such as judges and doctors, have been shown to be influenced by arbitrary starting points.
paras.D: Another is loss aversion: losing something hurts roughly twice as much as gaining the same thing pleases. For this reason, people often hold on to failing investments or refuse a fair risk, because they are more worried about what they might lose than excited about what they might win. Shops exploit the effect with free trials, since giving something up feels worse than never having had it.
paras.E: A third bias concerns memory. Because dramatic events are easier to recall, people overestimate the frequency of things they have seen in the news. Many fear air travel more than driving, though the statistics show that cars are far more dangerous per kilometre. The vivid image of a plane crash simply comes to mind more readily than the many small accidents on roads.
paras.F: Can biases be avoided? Training helps a little, but knowing about a bias does not make it disappear. More effective is to change the situation in which choices are made. Checklists, waiting a day before large purchases and asking someone with no stake in the outcome can all improve judgement. Organisations can also design options so that the sensible choice is the easy one, for example by enrolling employees in pension plans automatically.
paras.G: None of this means that intuition is worthless. Experts with years of practice, such as chess masters and experienced nurses, often make excellent snap judgements. The difficulty is knowing when to trust a feeling. As a general rule, intuition can be relied on in areas where we have had plenty of feedback, but should be questioned in unfamiliar and uncertain situations.

paras.A: There are about seven thousand languages in the world, but they are very unevenly spread. Roughly forty per cent have fewer than a thousand speakers, while a small number, such as Mandarin, Spanish and English, are used by hundreds of millions. Linguists estimate that, if present trends continue, around half of all languages could disappear by the end of this century.
paras.B: The causes are largely social. When parents believe that a regional or national language will give their children better chances at school and work, they stop speaking the smaller language at home. Within two or three generations, the youngest speakers no longer use it, and when the last elderly speakers die, the language disappears with them.
paras.C: Globalisation intensifies this pressure. Television, films and the internet are dominated by a few big languages, and young people who grow up with them may start to consider their own language old-fashioned. At the same time, migration to cities puts speakers of different languages together, and they usually choose a common one for daily life.
paras.D: What is lost when a language dies? Some argue that every language carries a unique way of describing the world, including knowledge of local plants, animals and weather that may not have been recorded elsewhere. A vocabulary can contain dozens of terms for the kinds of snow or the stages of a river's flood. Stories, songs and humour are also hard to translate.
paras.E: Others take a more practical view. They point out that a common language makes trade, science and travel easier, and that many speakers of small languages choose to change for sound reasons. From this perspective, preserving a language by force would be unfair to those who prefer to move on. The best approach, they say, is to support those who wish to continue, not to prevent change.
paras.F: Efforts to revive languages have had real successes. Hebrew, which was used mainly for prayer for centuries, became a living national language again. Welsh and Maori, helped by schools and radio broadcasts in the languages, have increased the number of young speakers. Technology can assist as well, through dictionaries and recordings kept by communities themselves.
paras.G: The future will probably be a mixture. Large languages will continue to expand, but many people will be bilingual or trilingual, using a global language for work and a local one for family and tradition. Whether the smallest languages survive will depend less on linguists than on the choices of their speakers and on the respect shown for them.

paras.A: Every society needs to organise time, and the most natural units come from the sky. A day is one turn of the Earth, a month is roughly one cycle of the moon, and a year is one journey round the sun. The difficulty is that these cycles do not fit neatly together: a year contains about 365 and a quarter days, and about twelve and a third lunar months.
paras.B: Early calendars were often based on the moon, because its phases are easy to observe. In a pure lunar calendar of twelve months, the year is about eleven days short, so the months slowly drift through the seasons. The Islamic calendar works this way, which is why Ramadan moves earlier each year. Other cultures, such as the ancient Babylonians, added an extra month every few years to keep the seasons in place.
paras.C: The Egyptians preferred a calendar of 365 days, divided into twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days. It was simple and useful for farming, since the flooding of the Nile occurred at about the same time each year. However, because the real year is slightly longer, the calendar gradually slipped out of line with the seasons.
paras.D: The Romans reformed their messy system under Julius Caesar in 46 BC. The new Julian calendar had 365 days and an extra 'leap day' every fourth year. This was a clever idea, but the average year was still about eleven minutes too long. By the sixteenth century, the error had grown to ten days, and the date of Easter, which depends on the spring equinox, was drifting.
paras.E: In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII introduced a correction. Ten days were removed from the calendar, and it was decided that century years such as 1700 and 1900 would not be leap years unless divisible by four hundred. This Gregorian calendar was accepted slowly: Protestant and Orthodox countries delayed for decades or centuries, and Russia adopted it only after the revolution of 1917.
paras.F: Today, the Gregorian calendar is used for civil purposes almost everywhere, while many communities still keep traditional calendars for religious festivals and cultural events. The Persian solar calendar, for instance, begins each year on the spring equinox, which is why Navruz is celebrated in many countries on about the 21st of March.
paras.G: Reformers have suggested improvements, such as a calendar of thirteen months of four weeks, but none has won general support. People are attached to the familiar rhythm of weeks and months, and changing it would affect everything from contracts to holidays. The calendar we use is therefore the product of astronomy, politics and habit in equal measure.

paras.A: In many countries, children are taught in a language that is not the one they speak at home. Immigrant children may attend schools in the national language, while in former colonies the language of instruction may be that of the former ruler. Educators have long debated how best to teach such children, and the question has become more pressing as societies grow more diverse.
paras.B: One approach is immersion, in which pupils are taught entirely in the new language from the first day, in the belief that the more they hear it, the faster they will learn. Another is bilingual education, in which pupils study some subjects in their home language and others in the second one. A third approach teaches in the home language at first and then gradually moves to the second.
paras.C: The research evidence is encouraging for bilingual programmes. Large studies in several countries have found that children who continue to develop their first language while learning the second often achieve as well as or better than those in immersion programmes by the later grades. A strong foundation in one language seems to transfer: concepts learned in one language can be expressed in another.
paras.D: The reasons are plausible. A child who cannot understand lessons falls behind in subjects such as mathematics and science, even if the child is intelligent, simply because the teaching is not understood. Learning to read in a familiar language is easier, and the skills gained, such as recognising sounds and patterns in print, can be applied to a second language later.
paras.E: Some fears about bilingualism have proved unfounded. For many years, people believed that speaking two languages confuses a child and delays development. Modern research shows that bilingual children may mix words at times, but their total vocabulary is typically equal to or larger than that of single-language children, and they often become skilled at changing between tasks.
paras.F: There are practical obstacles. Bilingual programmes need teachers who speak both languages, textbooks in several tongues and enough pupils from one language group to form a class. In schools where children speak a dozen different languages, offering lessons in each is impossible, and other kinds of support, such as extra language classes, are more realistic.
paras.G: Beyond test scores, there are cultural benefits. Children who see their home language respected at school tend to feel more confident, and families are more likely to take part in education. As societies become more mixed, the ability to use two languages is increasingly regarded as an asset, not a problem to be solved.

paras.A: Antibiotics, medicines that kill bacteria, were one of the great achievements of the twentieth century. After Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould could kill bacteria, and after penicillin entered use in the 1940s, infections that had once been deadly, such as pneumonia and blood poisoning, became treatable. Surgery, cancer treatment and childbirth all became much safer.
paras.B: The success, however, carries the seeds of a problem. Bacteria multiply very quickly, and in any large population, a few individuals may carry a chance change that allows them to survive a particular drug. When the drug kills the others, these survivors multiply and pass on the resistance, a clear example of natural selection occurring in real time.
paras.C: Human behaviour speeds the process. Doctors sometimes prescribe antibiotics for viral illnesses such as colds, against which they are useless, and patients who stop taking their tablets as soon as they feel better leave the strongest bacteria alive. In agriculture, large quantities of antibiotics are given to healthy animals to make them grow faster, which also encourages resistance.
paras.D: The consequences are already visible. The World Health Organization considers resistance one of the greatest threats to global health, and studies estimate that drug-resistant infections contribute to millions of deaths each year. Diseases such as tuberculosis are becoming harder and more expensive to treat, requiring many months of medicine with unpleasant side effects.
paras.E: New antibiotics are not arriving quickly enough. Developing a drug is costly, and because new antibiotics are kept in reserve to treat only the worst infections, they earn little money for the companies that produce them. As a result, many large pharmaceutical firms have left the field, and the number of new drugs discovered has declined.
paras.F: Several measures could help. Doctors can prescribe antibiotics only when necessary, hospitals can improve hygiene to prevent the spread of infections, and farms can reduce their use of the drugs. Governments might pay companies for developing new antibiotics regardless of how many are sold. Researchers are also exploring alternatives, such as viruses that attack bacteria and drugs that disarm rather than kill them.
paras.G: Individuals can play a part as well. Finishing the course of tablets, never sharing prescriptions and washing hands regularly all reduce the problem. Resistance is a shared challenge: bacteria do not respect borders, and a resistant strain that appears in one country can reach any other within days. Each of us therefore has a stake in the effectiveness of these medicines, and each of us shares the duty to use them carefully.

paras.A: By the middle of this century, the world's population is expected to approach ten billion, and food production will need to increase substantially. At the same time, farming itself is under pressure: it uses about half of the planet's habitable land, a large share of fresh water, and is responsible for a significant portion of greenhouse gas emissions. Farmers must therefore produce more with less harm.
paras.B: One response is precision agriculture. Tractors guided by satellites, drones that photograph fields and sensors in the soil provide information about exactly where crops need water, fertiliser or protection. Instead of treating a whole field in the same way, the farmer can apply inputs only where they are needed, saving money and reducing pollution.
paras.C: Another is the improvement of crops. Traditional breeding, supported by new genetic tools, can produce varieties that resist drought, salty soils or disease. In Central Asia, where water is scarce and soils are often salty, such varieties could be particularly valuable. Research on staple foods such as rice and wheat has already saved millions of people from hunger.
paras.D: A third approach is to grow food in new places and ways. Vertical farms stack layers of plants in buildings, using artificial light and recycled water, and can supply fresh vegetables to cities all year. They use very little land or water, but they need large amounts of electricity, and for now they are practical mainly for leafy greens and herbs, not for grain.
paras.E: Reducing waste may be as important as growing more. Roughly a third of all food produced is lost or thrown away, some of it spoiled between farm and market because of poor storage and transport, and some of it discarded by shops and households. Better refrigeration, packaging and planning could feed many people without using a single extra hectare.
paras.F: Diets matter too. Meat, especially beef, requires far more land and water than plants for each unit of food energy. If people in rich countries ate less meat, land would be released for other uses. Many scientists also support research into alternative proteins, such as foods made from plants or grown from cells, though their cost and acceptance are uncertain.
paras.G: No single idea will be enough. The future of farming will probably combine new technology with traditional knowledge, local solutions with global trade, and changes by producers with changes by consumers. paras.A: It is a common belief that more money leads to more happiness, and at low levels of income, the evidence supports it. People who cannot afford food, shelter or medicine are understandably unhappy, and surveys across many countries show that satisfaction with life rises steeply as incomes increase from poverty to a modest, secure level.
paras.B: Beyond that point, the relationship becomes weaker. Researchers have found that after basic needs and a degree of comfort are met, additional income produces smaller and smaller gains. A person earning a very high salary is, on average, somewhat happier than one with an average salary, but the difference is much less than the gap in their wealth might suggest.
paras.C: One explanation is adaptation. People quickly get used to improvements in their lives: a new car or a larger house gives pleasure at first, but the feeling fades within months, and the person begins to desire something better. Psychologists describe this as a 'hedonic treadmill', in which people run harder to stay in the same place.
paras.D: Comparison also plays a major part. Happiness depends not only on how much we have but on how it compares to what others have. If neighbours and colleagues become richer, our own wealth feels smaller, even if it has not changed. Social media may intensify the effect by showing a stream of other people's holidays and possessions.
paras.E: What, then, does lead to happiness? Studies repeatedly point to relationships. People who have close friends and family, and who spend time with them, report greater satisfaction than those who are wealthy but isolated. Meaningful work, good health, a sense of control over one's life and helping others are also strongly linked to wellbeing.
paras.F: Interestingly, the way money is spent matters. Experiments suggest that spending on experiences, such as a trip with friends, usually brings more lasting pleasure than spending on objects, and that spending money on other people can raise happiness more than spending the same amount on oneself.
paras.G: None of this suggests that money is unimportant. Financial security reduces worry and gives people choices. The lesson, rather, is that once basic needs are met, a rising income is a poor guide to a good life. Societies that want happy citizens may do better to invest in health, education and communities than to focus only on economic growth. Ultimately, each person must decide what a good life means, but the research gives a useful starting point for that conversation, and it deserves to be taken seriously by individuals and governments alike.

title: The Great Trade Cities of the Silk Road

paras.A: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean. Its most important points were the oasis cities where caravans rested, exchanged goods and bought supplies. Among them, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva became famous throughout the world for their wealth, learning and architecture.
paras.B: Samarkand lay at a crossing of routes and drew merchants from many lands. Its markets sold silk, paper, spices, glass and horses, and its craftsmen were known for their ceramics and metalwork. The city was destroyed by the Mongols in 1220, but it rose again, and under Timur in the fourteenth century it became the glittering capital of a great empire, filled with mosques and madrasas decorated with blue tiles.
paras.C: Bukhara, to the west, became a centre of religion and scholarship. Its madrasas trained thousands of students, and its libraries held works on medicine, mathematics and poetry. The city also contained covered bazaars, some of which still stand, where goldsmiths, carpet sellers and money-changers worked under domed roofs that protected them from the summer sun.
paras.D: Merchants carried far more than goods. Along the same routes travelled religions such as Buddhism, Christianity and Islam, technologies such as papermaking, and artistic styles. A scholar in Bukhara might read a text translated from Greek, and a painter in Samarkand might borrow patterns from China. In this way, the cities were centres of exchange of ideas as well as of commerce.
paras.E: The trade was also supported by institutions. Caravanserais, large inns with space for animals, were built along the roads to give travellers a safe place to rest. Rulers collected taxes on goods but also guaranteed security, since trade that was robbed or heavily taxed would go elsewhere. Money-changers and written promises of payment made it possible to do business over long distances.
paras.F: The decline came slowly. From the sixteenth century, European ships opened sea routes to Asia, which were cheaper for bulk goods, and political divisions made overland travel less safe. The oasis cities lost much of their wealth, although they remained centres of local trade and culture, and many of their monuments survived.
paras.G: Today, these cities attract visitors from all over the world, and the historic centres of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva have been recognised by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites. Their story reminds us that contact between peoples, though it has risks, has often been the source of progress and creativity. Many travellers also say that walking through the old streets, past the same walls once seen by merchants, gives a sense of history that no book can fully provide.

paras.A: For its first half-century, space exploration was the business of governments. The United States and the Soviet Union competed to launch satellites, send people into orbit and, in 1969, to land astronauts on the Moon. These programmes were enormously costly and were driven by national prestige and military rivalry as much as by scientific curiosity.
paras.B: In recent years, private companies have become major players. They launch satellites for communications, television and navigation, carry cargo to the International Space Station and, in some cases, carry astronauts. Companies led by wealthy entrepreneurs have also announced plans for tourism, mining and settlements on other worlds.
paras.C: The most striking change has been in price. Traditionally, rockets were used once and then discarded, which was like throwing away an aeroplane after a single flight. Some companies now land their rockets upright and reuse them, and this has cut the cost of putting a kilogram into orbit by a large factor. Cheaper launches have made it possible for universities and small countries to operate satellites.
paras.D: Supporters of private enterprise argue that competition promotes innovation and efficiency. Companies that must make a profit have a reason to cut costs and to develop new technologies quickly. Governments, they say, can then act as customers, buying services rather than owning every rocket, and concentrate their funds on science that has no commercial value.
paras.E: Critics raise several concerns. A handful of companies now control vital infrastructure, such as satellite networks, and decisions about their use can be made by a few individuals. The growth in the number of satellites also adds to the problem of space debris, makes astronomical observations harder, and raises questions about who is responsible for safety in orbit.
paras.F: Legal questions remain unanswered. An international treaty from 1967 says that no nation may claim the Moon or other bodies, but it does not clearly say whether a company may own the resources it extracts. Several countries have passed their own laws allowing such mining, while others believe that a common international agreement is needed.
paras.G: Probably the future will include both public and private effort. Governments are best suited to long-term research and exploration without immediate profit, while companies excel at making existing activities cheaper. Success will depend on rules that encourage innovation while protecting the space environment, which belongs, in a sense, to all humanity. Young people growing up today may well see the first permanent bases on the Moon, and the choices made now will shape how those bases are built, owned and shared.

paras.A: Much of what we do each day is not decided at the moment. Studies suggest that perhaps forty per cent of daily actions are habits, behaviour repeated in the same situation until it becomes automatic. We brush our teeth, take the same route to work and reach for a phone without conscious thought. Habits free the mind for other matters, but they can also trap us in patterns we would like to break.
paras.B: Researchers describe a habit as a loop with three parts. First comes a cue, such as the alarm clock or the end of a meal. Then comes the routine, the behaviour itself. Finally comes a reward, such as a pleasant taste or a feeling of relief, which tells the brain that the loop is worth remembering. With repetition, the cue alone triggers a craving for the reward.
paras.C: Brain studies show that as a behaviour becomes a habit, activity moves from regions involved in decision-making to deeper areas that handle automatic patterns. This is why habits can continue even after we no longer want the reward. A person who has stopped enjoying a snack may still eat it every afternoon, because the cue of the clock triggers the routine without any real choice.
paras.D: It is often claimed that it takes twenty-one days to form a habit, but the evidence does not support this. One study that followed volunteers as they adopted new behaviours found that the time varied from about two months on average to much longer for difficult actions. Missing a single day, however, did not seriously damage progress, which is encouraging for anyone who is trying.
paras.E: How can we build a good habit? Experts suggest starting small, so small that it is difficult to fail, such as doing two push-ups or reading one page. Attaching the new behaviour to an existing one, for example flossing right after brushing, provides a ready-made cue. Making the desired action easy, by laying out running shoes the night before, also helps.
paras.F: Breaking a bad habit is harder, since the cue and craving remain. Rather than relying on willpower, it is more effective to remove cues, for instance by keeping sweets out of the house, and to substitute a different routine that gives a similar reward, such as chewing gum or drinking water. Telling friends about the goal can add useful social pressure.
paras.G: Understanding habit shows why good intentions often fail: willpower is limited, but environments are constant. Those who change their surroundings and routines, rather than simply trying harder, are the most likely to succeed. In this sense, we become what we repeatedly do, and small actions repeated daily can shape a life.

paras.A: In most parts of the world, people are living longer and having fewer children. As a result, the average age of populations is rising. Japan, Italy and Germany already have a large proportion of citizens over sixty-five, and many other countries, including China and Uzbekistan's neighbours, will follow in the coming decades. This demographic change is among the most important trends of the century.
paras.B: The cause is a success story. Better food, clean water, vaccination and medicine have greatly reduced early deaths, and in many countries, life expectancy has risen by more than twenty years since 1950. At the same time, as women gain education and careers, and as children are more likely to survive, families choose to have fewer children.
paras.C: The economic consequences can be serious. A smaller share of the population is of working age, so there are fewer people to pay taxes that fund pensions and healthcare. Governments face higher costs for hospitals and care homes, and some businesses struggle to find workers. Housing, transport and shops must also be adapted to the needs of older customers.
paras.D: Some countries respond by raising the retirement age, which makes sense when people are healthy for longer. Others encourage more women and older people to work, or invite workers from abroad. Technology can help as well: robots already assist in some Japanese care homes, and devices can monitor the health of elderly people living alone.
paras.E: There is, however, another side to the story. Older people possess experience, and many contribute through work, volunteering and looking after grandchildren. Some economists speak of a 'longevity dividend': if people remain healthy and active, the extra years can be productive rather than a burden. The decisive factor is health, not simply age.
paras.F: Different regions face different problems. Wealthy countries are ageing after they have become rich, while some developing countries will grow old before they have built strong pension and health systems. Those countries have a short time in which to prepare, and many experts urge them to invest now in basic healthcare and savings schemes.
paras.G: Society will need new attitudes as well as new policies. If older people are seen only as dependants, their talents will be wasted. If, instead, communities provide opportunities for learning, work and friendship at every age, a longer life could be one of humanity's greatest achievements rather than a challenge to be feared. Planning for an older society is therefore not only a duty to the elderly, but an investment in the future of every generation that will one day grow old.

title: Hidden Water: The Footprint of What We Use

paras.A: When we think about water use, we usually imagine drinking, washing and watering the garden. But these direct uses are small compared with the water needed to produce the things we buy. The 'water footprint' of a product is the total amount of fresh water used in making it, from growing the raw materials to manufacturing and transport.
paras.B: Food has the largest footprint. Producing a kilogram of wheat takes roughly a thousand litres of water, much of it as rainfall absorbed by the plants. A kilogram of beef takes many times more, because the animal eats grass and grain over its lifetime, and estimates are around fifteen thousand litres. A cup of coffee, taking into account the water needed to grow and process the beans, requires well over a hundred litres.
paras.C: Industry and clothing also use a lot. A single cotton shirt may require about 2,500 litres, and making a smartphone needs many more through mining, manufacturing and the production of electricity. Because most of this water is used far from the shop where the product is sold, shoppers rarely see the consequences.
paras.D: This leads to the idea of 'virtual water': when a country imports a product, it also imports the water used to make it. A dry country can therefore save its own water by importing water-hungry goods and growing less thirsty crops. On the other hand, countries that export such goods may drain their own rivers and aquifers to supply customers elsewhere.
paras.E: The Aral Sea disaster shows the risk. Huge quantities of river water were diverted to irrigate cotton, and the sea lost most of its volume in a few decades. Today, many regions face similar pressures, as demand for water rises with populations and incomes, and climate change makes rainfall less reliable.
paras.F: What can be done? Farmers can use drip irrigation, which delivers water to the roots, and grow crops suited to the climate. Companies can measure and report their footprints, and governments can set prices for water that reflect its scarcity. Consumers, meanwhile, can reduce waste of food, which wastes the water behind it.
paras.G: Awareness is a first step. Knowing that a hamburger, a shirt or a phone has a hidden cost in water encourages more thoughtful choices. No one expects people to calculate every purchase, but a basic understanding of where water goes can make societies more careful about a resource on which all life depends. Small habits, repeated by millions of people, can add up to large savings of a resource that is far more limited than most of us imagine.

paras.A: The word 'democracy' comes from two Greek words meaning 'rule by the people'. It is usually traced to the city of Athens, where, in the fifth century BC, male citizens gathered in an open assembly to debate and vote on laws, wars and taxes. Compared with the monarchies and empires around it, this was a radical experiment, and it has influenced political thinking ever since.
paras.B: Athenian democracy was direct: citizens voted on issues themselves, rather than choosing representatives. Officials were often selected by lot, a lottery, on the principle that any citizen was capable of serving. Yet the system had severe limits. Women, slaves and foreigners, who made up most of the population, were excluded, so that perhaps one in five inhabitants could take part.
paras.C: Elsewhere, other forms of shared government existed. In parts of ancient India, assemblies of leading men made decisions in some small states, and many societies had councils of elders who advised their rulers. The Roman Republic developed a system of elected officials and a senate, although power was concentrated among wealthy families, and the republic eventually gave way to emperors.
paras.D: In medieval Europe, ideas of limited government grew slowly. In 1215, English barons forced King John to sign Magna Carta, a document that stated that even the king was subject to the law. Parliaments developed, at first as meetings where rulers asked nobles and townspeople for money, and later as bodies with real power to make laws and control taxes.
paras.E: The modern form of democracy, based on elected representatives, took shape during the eighteenth century. The American and French revolutions declared that governments derive their authority from the consent of the governed. Even so, the right to vote was restricted to property owners and men for another hundred years or more, and women in many countries won it only in the twentieth century.
paras.F: Today, most countries hold elections, but they differ greatly in how free and fair they are. Political scientists emphasise that democracy requires more than voting: it also needs independent courts, a free press, the protection of minorities and the possibility of a peaceful change of government. Without these, elections may be a mere appearance.
paras.G: Democracy faces challenges in every age, including low trust in politicians and the spread of false information. Its defenders argue that, for all its faults, it has a unique strength: it allows mistakes to be corrected without violence. As the old saying goes, it may be the worst form of government except for all the others that have been tried.

paras.A: For centuries, museums have been places where valuable objects are collected, preserved and displayed. Visitors walked through halls, read small labels and, if they were lucky, listened to a guide. Today, digital technology is changing this experience, and it is also raising questions about what a museum is for.
paras.B: One obvious change is access. Many museums have photographed their collections in high detail and placed them online, so that anyone with an internet connection can zoom in on a painting's brushstrokes or turn a sculpture on the screen. Objects that spend most of their time in storage because they are too fragile or numerous to display can now be seen by the public for the first time.
paras.C: Inside the buildings, technology is changing displays. Visitors may point a phone at an object and see a reconstruction of how it once looked, hear the voice of a craftsman describing how it was made or watch an ancient ruin rise again in three dimensions. In some museums, interactive tables let children design their own patterns or test scientific ideas by touch.
paras.D: Technology also helps research and preservation. Scanners can reveal drawings hidden beneath layers of paint, and computer analysis can identify the materials in a pot or a manuscript. Detailed three-dimensional copies of damaged objects can be made so that experts can study them, while the originals are protected from handling.
paras.E: Not everyone welcomes the changes. Critics fear that museums may turn into entertainment parks, with spectacular effects that distract from the objects themselves. Others note that the quality of a screen image, however sharp, cannot convey the size, weight or presence of a real thing, and that this presence is the particular value of a museum.
paras.F: There are also debates about ownership. Many objects in European museums were taken from other regions during colonial times, and countries of origin have requested their return. Digital copies are sometimes proposed as a compromise, but those who ask for the objects reply that a copy is not the same as the original, whose home they consider to be elsewhere.
paras.G: The most successful museums are likely to combine both worlds, using technology to invite people in and to explain, and the real objects to inspire wonder. After all, no matter how good the screen, many people still want to stand in front of the real thing and to feel connected, across the centuries, with those who made it. Whatever the format, the central aim remains to help visitors ask questions and to give them a reason to care about the past.

paras.A: Noise is the most familiar form of pollution, yet it is often ignored. Traffic, aircraft, building work and loud music are part of everyday life in cities, and many people believe they have become used to them. Scientists, however, have found that unwanted sound affects health and wellbeing even when we think we are not paying attention.
paras.B: Sound is measured in decibels. A quiet library has about 30 decibels, normal conversation about 60 and a busy road about 80. The scale is logarithmic, so an increase of ten decibels makes a sound seem about twice as loud. Prolonged exposure to levels above 85 decibels can damage hearing, which is why workers in factories and airports are given ear protection.
paras.C: The effects are not limited to hearing loss. Long-term exposure to noise has been linked to high blood pressure, heart disease and disturbed sleep. Even when people do not wake up, their bodies react to noises at night by releasing stress hormones, and poor sleep in turn affects mood and concentration. The World Health Organization considers noise a significant environmental risk to health.
paras.D: Children are particularly vulnerable. Studies of schools near airports and busy roads show that pupils there often have more difficulty reading and remembering, probably because noise interrupts concentration and makes it harder to hear speech. When a new airport replaced an old one in one study, the children near the old site improved, while those near the new one did worse.
paras.E: Animals suffer as well. Whales and dolphins depend on sound to navigate and communicate, and the engines of ships interfere with them. Birds in noisy cities often sing at a higher pitch or at different times of day in order to be heard. Some species avoid noisy areas entirely, which reduces the habitat available to them.
paras.F: Solutions exist. Quieter road surfaces, electric vehicles and barriers along motorways reduce traffic noise, and flight paths can be arranged to avoid dense housing. Cities can plan their zones so that homes and schools are not built beside industry, and strict limits can be enforced at night. Better insulation in windows also helps individual families.
paras.G: Noise also has a positive opposite: quiet. Research suggests that a few minutes of quiet can lower stress, and people increasingly value parks and 'quiet areas' in cities. Protecting such places is no luxury; it is a way of caring for the physical and mental health of everyone who lives nearby. Small steps, such as lowering the volume of music and choosing quiet equipment, add up when many people take them together.

title: Secrets and Codes: The Story of Cryptography

paras.A: People have always had reasons to keep messages secret: generals planning battles, merchants protecting prices, lovers hiding their feelings. The science of secret writing is called cryptography, and its history is a long contest between those who make codes and those who try to break them.
paras.B: One of the earliest known methods is the Caesar cipher, said to have been used by Julius Caesar. Each letter in a message is replaced by the letter a fixed number of places further along the alphabet, so that with a shift of three, A becomes D. It is easy to use, but also easy to break, since an enemy need only try the twenty-five possible shifts.
paras.C: Arab scholars made a breakthrough in the ninth century. Al-Kindi, a philosopher in Baghdad, noticed that in any language, some letters appear more often than others. By counting the frequency of symbols in a coded message, a codebreaker could guess which symbols stood for the most common letters. This technique, called frequency analysis, defeated simple substitution codes for centuries.
paras.D: Codemakers responded with more complicated systems. In the sixteenth century, ciphers used several alphabets in rotation, and the method was thought unbreakable for about three hundred years. In the twentieth century, machines such as the German Enigma scrambled messages in billions of ways, and the work of mathematicians who broke it, at Bletchley Park in Britain, is believed to have shortened the Second World War.
paras.E: Computers changed the field again. Modern encryption relies on mathematical problems that are easy to perform in one direction but extremely hard to reverse, such as multiplying two large prime numbers. A system called public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met exchange secure messages, because one key for locking can be shared openly while the key for unlocking is kept private.
paras.F: Today, encryption protects bank transfers, online shopping and private messages for billions of people, often without their noticing. It has also become the subject of political debate. Governments argue that criminals can hide behind strong encryption, while privacy campaigners reply that weakening it would endanger everyone's security.
paras.G: The story of cryptography shows an enduring pattern: each advance by the makers is followed by progress among the breakers. The next challenge may come from quantum computers, which could one day solve problems that are impossible today, and researchers are already designing new codes to resist them. For ordinary users, the practical lesson is to use strong passwords and keep software updated, since even the best codes fail when people are careless with their keys.
