paras.A: Throughout history, people have moved from one place to another. Today, roughly 280 million people, a little over three per cent of the world's population, live in a country other than the one in which they were born. Behind each figure is a personal story, but researchers have identified some common patterns in why people leave their homes and where they go.
paras.B: Economists often speak of 'push' and 'pull' factors. Push factors are the conditions that drive people away, such as poverty, unemployment, war, persecution and natural disasters. Pull factors are the attractions of the destination, such as better wages, safety, education and the presence of relatives. Most migrants are influenced by a combination of both.
paras.C: Work is the most common reason. Millions of people move to earn more and send money home, and these payments, called remittances, are a major source of income in many countries. For some economies, they exceed the value of foreign aid. In Central Asia, remittances from workers abroad form a large share of household income in several countries.
paras.D: Not all migration is voluntary. Some 100 million people are displaced by conflict, violence or disasters, and most of them stay within their own countries or move to neighbouring ones. Refugees, people who have crossed a border to escape persecution, have special protection under international law, but in practice, they often live for years in camps or temporary housing.
paras.E: Migration has costs and benefits for both sides. Destination countries gain workers, skills and cultural diversity, and in ageing societies, migrants help to fill jobs and support the economy. However, rapid change can raise tensions, especially where housing and jobs are scarce, and communities need time and help to adjust.
paras.F: The countries that migrants leave also experience mixed effects. They benefit from remittances and from the skills that returning migrants bring, but they may lose doctors, teachers and engineers, a problem sometimes called the 'brain drain'. Some governments encourage their citizens to work abroad temporarily, while trying to create opportunities at home.
paras.G: Experts generally agree that migration will continue, and may increase as climate change affects living conditions in some regions. Managing it fairly requires cooperation between countries, respect for the rights of migrants and honest public discussion based on facts rather than fear. For the migrants themselves, the decision to leave is rarely easy, because it means leaving family, language and familiar surroundings behind in the hope of a better life. Many also keep close ties with their homeland, visiting when they can and supporting projects in their home towns.

paras.A: We tend to think of play as something that belongs to childhood and has little value besides amusement. Researchers who study child development take a very different view. They see play as the main way in which young humans, and many young animals, learn about the world, practise skills and begin to understand other people.
paras.B: Play takes many forms. Babies play with sounds and objects, toddlers pretend that a box is a car, and older children play games with rules, such as football or chess. Each stage develops different abilities: movement, imagination, language and cooperation. In pretend play, children try on adult roles and learn to see things from another point of view.
paras.C: Physical play is especially important. Running, climbing and chasing build strength and coordination, and they help children learn how to judge risk. Some safety experts now argue that protecting children too much from small risks, such as climbing a low tree, may make them less able to cope with danger later. Outdoor play also exposes children to light and fresh air.
paras.D: Social skills grow through games. To play together, children must take turns, negotiate rules and handle disappointment when they lose. These lessons are difficult to teach by instruction, but easy to absorb when something enjoyable is at stake. Studies suggest that children with plenty of opportunities for free play tend to be better at managing their emotions.
paras.E: Unfortunately, free play is under pressure. In many countries, children spend more time in organised activities, homework and in front of screens, and less time playing outdoors without adult direction. Researchers have recorded a long-term fall in the amount of unstructured play, and some link it with rising levels of anxiety among the young.
paras.F: Adults need to play too. Games, hobbies and sport relieve stress and keep the mind flexible, and some companies encourage playful approaches in order to produce creative ideas. Anthropologists note that all cultures have games, which suggests that play fulfils a deep human need.
paras.G: What can schools and parents do? They can protect time for unstructured play, provide safe spaces and simple materials such as boxes, sticks and sand, and resist the temptation to organise every minute. A child who is bored may complain, but boredom is often the beginning of invention. Play is not the opposite of learning; it is one of its oldest forms. Teachers who allow even a short break for free play during the school day often find that pupils return to lessons more alert and cooperative.

paras.A: For centuries, the testimony of an eyewitness has been regarded as strong evidence in courts of law. A person who says, 'I saw him do it', is usually believed. Psychologists who study memory, however, have shown that human recollection is far less reliable than most people assume, and that confident witnesses can be completely mistaken.
paras.B: The main reason is that memory is not a recording. When we remember an event, we rebuild it from fragments, filling gaps with expectations and later information. Each time we recall a memory, it may be slightly changed before it is stored again. Over weeks and months, details can fade or be replaced, yet the person may feel more certain than ever.
paras.C: The classic experiments were carried out by Elizabeth Loftus in the 1970s. She showed volunteers a film of a traffic accident and then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other. Other volunteers were asked the same question using the word 'hit'. Those who heard 'smashed' gave higher estimates of speed, and a week later, many remembered seeing broken glass that did not exist.
paras.D: Stress and violence can make recall worse, not better. When a weapon is present, witnesses tend to focus on it and remember the face of the attacker poorly, a phenomenon known as 'weapon focus'. Identifying strangers is especially difficult, particularly across ethnic groups, because people are less skilled at telling apart faces they see less often.
paras.E: The consequences can be grave. In the United States, studies of people later cleared by DNA evidence have shown that mistaken eyewitness identification played a role in a large majority of wrongful convictions. Many of these witnesses were sincere, which makes their testimony all the more convincing to juries.
paras.F: Reforms are therefore being introduced. Police are advised to record a witness's confidence immediately, to avoid leading questions and to show suspects in a line-up one at a time, not all together, so that the witness compares each person with memory rather than with the others. The person conducting the line-up should not know who the suspect is, to avoid giving unconscious hints.
paras.G: This does not mean that witnesses should be ignored; many are accurate. It means that their evidence should be treated with care and checked against other proof. Understanding the limits of memory is not only important for courts, but also for ordinary life, where we often argue with friends and relatives who remember the same event differently.

paras.A: Wind and solar power are growing quickly, yet they share a weakness: they produce electricity only when the wind blows and the sun shines. Demand for power, on the other hand, is highest in the morning and evening, often when solar panels are idle. If renewable energy is to supply most of our electricity, we need ways to store it until it is needed.
paras.B: The most familiar answer is the battery. Lithium-ion batteries, similar to those in phones and electric cars, are now installed alongside solar and wind farms in many countries. Their cost has fallen by roughly ninety per cent in a decade, and they respond within a fraction of a second, which helps to keep the grid stable. They are best suited to storing energy for a few hours.
paras.C: For longer periods, other methods are needed. The oldest and most widespread is pumped hydropower. When electricity is cheap, water is pumped uphill into a reservoir; when power is needed, the water flows down through turbines, generating electricity. This system accounts for most of the world's stored energy, but it requires suitable mountains and valleys and large areas of land.
paras.D: Researchers are exploring many other ideas. Some use surplus electricity to compress air in underground caverns, to be released later to drive turbines. Others heat large tanks of molten salt or sand, which keep their warmth for days. Still others use electricity to split water into hydrogen, a fuel that can be stored for months and burned or used in fuel cells when required.
paras.E: Each approach has drawbacks. Batteries require metals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel, the mining of which can damage environments and communities if not properly managed. Hydrogen production wastes a considerable share of the energy, and storing the gas safely is difficult. Compressed air needs special geology, and heat storage is usually only practical for industry.
paras.F: Storage is not the only solution. A grid connected over wide areas can move electricity from where it is windy to where it is calm. Consumers can also help by shifting their use, for example by charging vehicles at night or running washing machines when the sun is shining. Smart meters and variable prices encourage such flexibility.
paras.G: No single technology will do everything. The most likely future is a combination of batteries for short periods, other forms of storage for longer ones, strong grids and flexible demand. Because the sun and wind are free and abundant, solving the problem of storage could make clean electricity cheap and reliable for everyone.

paras.A: Not long ago, vegetarians were a small minority in most countries, and vegan restaurants were hard to find. Today, supermarkets sell plant-based burgers, milks and cheeses, and surveys suggest that a growing number of people are reducing their consumption of meat and dairy products. Their reasons include health, animal welfare and concern for the environment.
paras.B: The environmental argument is strong. Livestock farming is estimated to produce around fifteen per cent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, and it uses a very large part of the world's farmland, much of it to grow feed for animals. Producing a unit of protein from beef takes many times more land and water than producing the same amount from beans or lentils.
paras.C: The health evidence is more complicated. Studies show that diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains and pulses are associated with lower risks of heart disease and some cancers. Yet 'plant-based' does not automatically mean healthy: chips, sweet drinks and heavily processed meat substitutes can be high in salt, sugar and fat. The quality of the diet matters more than the label.
paras.D: Nutritionists note that a plant-based diet can supply nearly everything the body needs, but some nutrients require attention. Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods, so strict vegans need supplements. Iron, calcium, zinc and omega-3 fats also need planning, which is why children, pregnant women and older people should seek advice before making large changes.
paras.E: For many people, a complete change is not necessary. Flexitarians, who eat mostly plants but occasionally include meat or fish, can gain many of the benefits. Traditional cuisines offer inspiration: many dishes in Central Asia, the Mediterranean and India are built around vegetables, grains and pulses, with meat as a flavour or a treat.
paras.F: Critics raise other points. Farmers who raise animals fear for their livelihoods, and in dry or mountainous areas, grazing may be the only way to produce food. Some also argue that the modern meat substitutes are expensive, highly processed and designed by large corporations. Supporters reply that, as sales grow, prices will fall and new products will improve.
paras.G: The trend is likely to continue, supported by cost, technology and changing tastes. The most realistic aim is probably not a world without meat, but a world in which meat is eaten less often and produced more responsibly. Even a modest shift by millions of people could make a measurable difference. Whatever choice a person makes, variety, fresh ingredients and moderation remain sensible guidelines.

paras.A: Archaeology once meant digging with spades and brushes to uncover the remains of the past. The method is still essential, but the discipline has been transformed by new technologies that allow researchers to find sites without disturbing the ground, and to extract far more information from what they discover.
paras.B: One of the most powerful tools is lidar, a system that fires laser pulses from an aircraft and measures how long they take to return. The data can be processed to remove the trees and show the shape of the land beneath. In Central America, lidar revealed thousands of previously unknown Maya structures, including roads and fortifications, hidden under dense forest.
paras.C: Satellite images offer another view. Differences in the colour or height of crops can reveal buried walls, and photographs taken from space have helped to locate ancient canals and settlements in deserts. Ground-penetrating radar and magnetic surveys can map foundations below the surface, allowing archaeologists to decide where to dig, or whether to avoid digging at all.
paras.D: Laboratory science has been equally important. Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of a form of carbon in organic materials such as wood and bone, giving ages up to about fifty thousand years. Analysis of chemicals in teeth and bones can reveal what ancient people ate and where they grew up. Genetic studies of ancient DNA have shown how populations moved and mixed.
paras.E: Technology also helps with preservation and sharing. Three-dimensional scanning produces precise records of sites at risk from war, looting or climate change, and in some cases, it has made it possible to reconstruct monuments that were destroyed. Online databases allow researchers around the world to compare finds without travelling.
paras.F: Challenges accompany these advances. The same tools can help looters to find sites, and the large quantities of data must be stored and interpreted by trained specialists. Some scholars worry that excitement about technology may overshadow the careful study of context, which remains the foundation of the field: an object removed without recording where it lay loses most of its meaning.
paras.G: The future of archaeology will probably combine the old and the new. Machines may discover where to look and measure what is found, but it is people who ask questions, link evidence and tell the story. As methods improve, our knowledge of how our ancestors lived will deepen, and sometimes it will surprise us. Training new archaeologists in both field methods and digital skills is therefore becoming a priority for universities around the world.

paras.A: Every country organises schooling in its own way, and international tests have made it possible to compare results. Every few years, thousands of fifteen-year-olds in dozens of countries take the same tests in reading, mathematics and science. The rankings attract attention from newspapers and politicians, and countries such as Finland, Singapore and South Korea are often studied for their results.
paras.B: The systems that perform well differ greatly. In Singapore, teaching is highly structured and demanding, with a strong focus on mathematics and regular testing. In Finland, children start school at seven, have little homework and few standardised tests, but teachers are carefully selected, well trained and trusted to design lessons. Clearly, there is no single recipe.
paras.C: Researchers have nevertheless found some common features. High-performing systems usually attract strong candidates to teaching, give them thorough training and offer them time for professional development. They set clear and ambitious expectations for all pupils, not just those who find learning easy, and they pay attention to weak students early, before they fall far behind.
paras.D: Money matters, but less than might be expected. Above a certain level of spending, extra funds are not clearly linked to better results; how the money is used is more important. Smaller classes help in the early years, though they are costly, and some studies suggest that improving the quality of teaching has a larger effect for the same price.
paras.E: Family background has an enormous influence everywhere, but its strength differs. In some countries, a child from a poor family is far more likely to do badly than a child from a rich one, while in others, the gap is smaller. Systems that provide strong support for disadvantaged pupils and avoid sorting children into different schools too early tend to be fairer.
paras.F: There are also warnings against copying other countries blindly. Culture, history and expectations about work and family shape education, and an idea that succeeds in one place may fail in another. Intense pressure to achieve high scores, in some countries, has been linked to stress and unhappiness among students, so test results are not the only measure of success.
paras.G: Education should prepare young people for work, for citizenship and for a good life. International comparisons are valuable because they offer ideas and challenge assumptions, but they cannot tell us what we want from schools. That question is for each society to answer for itself, while learning from others. Teachers, parents and students themselves should have a voice in that conversation, because they understand daily life in school better than any ranking table.

paras.A: In 1830, a passenger railway opened between Liverpool and Manchester in England. Within a few decades, tracks had spread across Europe, North America and India, and by 1900, hundreds of thousands of kilometres of line existed worldwide. Few inventions have changed daily life so quickly and so thoroughly.
paras.B: The most obvious effect was speed. Before railways, the fastest way to travel overland was by horse, at perhaps thirty kilometres in a day on a coach. Trains could cover that distance in less than an hour. Journeys that had taken weeks were reduced to days, and goods and mail travelled with a regularity never seen before.
paras.C: Railways transformed economies. Heavy goods such as coal, grain and iron could now be carried cheaply over long distances, which allowed factories to grow and farmers to sell in distant cities. Towns that had a station prospered, and those that were bypassed often declined. Railway construction itself employed hundreds of thousands of workers and created demand for steel and machinery.
paras.D: The effects on time and place were surprising. Each town used to keep its own local time based on the sun, but timetables made this impractical, and railway companies introduced standard time across whole regions. Newspapers could be distributed on the same day, and people could live in the suburbs and travel into the city to work, which changed the shape of cities.
paras.E: Railways also changed politics and war. Governments could send armies quickly to defend borders or put down rebellions, and the Russian expansion in Central Asia was assisted by the Transcaspian railway, which reached Samarkand in 1888. Linking distant regions helped to build national identities, but it also made colonial control easier.
paras.F: There were costs. Building lines across mountains and deserts was dangerous, and many workers died. Engines burnt coal and covered cities in smoke. Land was taken from communities along the route, and the arrival of the railway sometimes harmed local crafts that could not compete with factory goods carried from far away.
paras.G: Today, railways are enjoying a revival. Electric trains emit far less carbon dioxide per passenger than cars or aeroplanes, and high-speed lines in Japan, China and Europe compete successfully with air travel on medium distances. After nearly two centuries, this old technology may help to solve a modern problem. Many old stations have been preserved as museums or markets, reminding us of the age when the whole world seemed to be moving faster for the first time, and of how much a single invention could change.

paras.A: The human body contains trillions of microbes, tiny living things such as bacteria, fungi and viruses. Most live in the large intestine, and together they are known as the gut microbiome. For many years, these organisms were regarded mainly as germs that cause disease, but scientists now understand that most are harmless and many are essential to our health.

They make some vitamins, and they train the immune system to tell the difference between dangerous invaders and harmless food. A balanced community also crowds out harmful bacteria by taking up space and nutrients.
paras.C: Each person's microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. It begins to form at birth, when babies receive microbes from their mothers, and is shaped by feeding, medicines and environment. By the age of three, it resembles that of an adult. Diet has a strong influence: people who eat a wide range of plant foods tend to have more diverse communities, which is generally seen as a sign of health.
paras.D: Research suggests links between the microbiome and many conditions, including obesity, allergies, diabetes and bowel disease. Some studies even point to a connection with mood, since the gut and brain communicate through nerves and chemicals. In one famous experiment, mice that received microbes from obese animals gained more weight than those that received microbes from lean ones.
paras.E: Such findings have inspired treatments. Doctors have successfully treated certain severe infections by transferring microbes from the faeces of a healthy donor into the patient, restoring a balanced community. Probiotics, products containing live bacteria, and prebiotics, which feed the existing ones, are widely sold, though evidence for their benefits in healthy people is often limited.
paras.F: Scientists urge caution. Most studies show association, not cause, and it is hard to tell whether changes in the microbiome produce an illness or result from it. The variety of individuals makes it difficult to say what a 'healthy' microbiome is. Claims made by companies that sell tests and supplements often run ahead of the evidence.
paras.G: The most reliable advice is simple. Eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains, use antibiotics only when necessary and avoid too many highly processed foods. As research continues, the microbiome may one day lead to personal treatments, but already it has changed how we think of ourselves: not as single organisms, but as ecosystems.

paras.A: Music exists in every known human society. People sing to babies, march to drums, dance at weddings and mourn with slow melodies. Yet it is puzzling that we should spend so much time on something that is not obviously needed for survival. Scientists and philosophers have long asked why music exists and how it affects us.
paras.B: One theory is that music evolved to strengthen social bonds. Singing and dancing together require coordination, and they release chemicals in the brain that create a feeling of closeness. Groups that made music together may have cooperated better and survived more often. Another idea is that music grew from the sounds that mothers make to calm their babies, which are similar in many cultures.
paras.C: Is music a universal language? In some respects, it is. Listeners from very different backgrounds can often tell whether a piece is meant to be happy or sad, and lullabies around the world share features such as slow tempo and gentle repetition. However, many details are learned. What sounds pleasant in one culture, such as a particular scale or rhythm, may seem strange in another.
paras.D: Music has a powerful effect on emotions. A well-loved song can bring tears or send shivers down the spine, and brain scans show that listening to favourite music activates regions linked to pleasure, the same ones that respond to food and other rewards. Composers create this effect partly by manipulating expectation, building tension and then resolving it, sometimes with a surprise.
paras.E: Learning an instrument appears to benefit the brain. Studies show that children who receive music lessons often improve in memory, attention and language skills, although it is not certain whether music causes the improvement or whether children who take lessons already differ in other ways. Adults who play also appear to retain mental sharpness well into old age.
paras.F: Music is increasingly used in health care. Hospitals play it to reduce anxiety before operations, and music therapists work with patients recovering from strokes or living with dementia. Remarkably, people who have forgotten much of their past can sometimes still sing songs from their youth, and the experience seems to bring comfort and a feeling of identity.
paras.G: Technology has changed how we listen. Streaming services give instant access to millions of songs, and software allows anyone to compose at home. Yet the heart of music remains the same: it is a way for people to share feeling and to feel connected. Perhaps that explains why, despite the lack of an obvious practical purpose, no society has ever done without it.

title: From Waste to Resource: the Circular Economy

paras.A: For most of the industrial age, the economy has worked in a straight line: companies take raw materials from the earth, make products, sell them and, when the products wear out, throw them away. This 'take, make, dispose' model has produced great wealth, but it also creates mountains of waste and uses up resources faster than nature can renew them.
paras.B: The 'circular economy' proposes a different idea. Instead of treating waste as the end of the line, it designs products so that materials stay in use for as long as possible, and the waste of one process becomes the raw material of another. This is how natural systems work: in a forest, nothing is wasted, since fallen leaves feed the soil from which new plants grow.
paras.C: In practice, a circular economy involves several strategies. Products can be designed to last longer and to be repaired easily. They can be shared or rented instead of owned, as when a community owns one drill for many households. When they reach the end of their life, they can be taken apart and their components reused or recycled into new goods.
paras.D: Some companies have already adopted such ideas. Makers of carpets lease their products and take them back for recycling, and manufacturers of phones offer repair services and refurbished models. Cities collect food waste and turn it into compost and biogas, and some industrial parks arrange for the steam or by-products of one factory to be used by its neighbours.
paras.E: The benefits could be considerable. Studies estimate that circular practices could reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs in repair and recycling and make countries less dependent on imported materials. For consumers, durable and repairable products can save money over time, even if the initial price is higher.
paras.F: There are obstacles. Many products are designed to be difficult to repair, with glued components or special tools, and mixed materials, such as plastics combined with metal, are hard to separate. Recycling often produces material of lower quality, and it requires energy. Existing laws and taxes sometimes favour new materials over recycled ones.
paras.G: Governments can help by requiring that products be repairable, by making producers responsible for the waste they create and by taxing pollution rather than work. Consumers can contribute by choosing durable goods and repairing instead of replacing. A fully circular economy may never be reached, but each step in that direction reduces the burden on the planet. Over time, such changes in habit and design could make waste a rare thing, and resources something we keep rather than lose.

paras.A: Society celebrates success, yet many of the greatest advances came through repeated failure. Thomas Edison is said to have tested thousands of materials before finding a filament for the light bulb that could last, and the story of penicillin began with an accident in a laboratory. Researchers on innovation increasingly argue that failure is not the opposite of progress but a necessary part of it.
paras.B: The reason is that, in new fields, nobody knows in advance what will work. The only way to find out is to try. Companies that encourage experiments accept that most will fail, but a few successes may more than repay the cost. Venture capitalists, who invest in new businesses, expect the majority of their investments to lose money and rely on a handful of winners.
paras.C: However, not all failures are equal. Experts distinguish between careless failure, which results from ignoring known rules, and intelligent failure, which occurs when a well-prepared experiment at the edge of knowledge does not work. The first should be prevented, while the second should be valued, because it produces information that others can use.
paras.D: Fear of failure can block learning. If people expect to be blamed, they hide their mistakes, and the organisation loses the chance to correct them. Aviation provides a good contrast: the industry encourages pilots and engineers to report errors and near-misses without punishment, and the information is analysed and shared. This culture is widely credited with the large improvement in air safety.
paras.E: Some firms have begun to treat failure openly. A few hold meetings in which staff describe their mistakes, and some publish lists of projects that were abandoned and the lessons learned. In science, journals have also started to publish 'negative results', studies in which an idea was tested and found wrong, so that other researchers do not waste time repeating them.
paras.F: Failure should not be romanticised. It can be painful and expensive, and not everyone can afford to take risks; a person with little money cannot easily fail and try again. Societies that offer a safety net, such as fair bankruptcy laws and unemployment support, may therefore encourage more entrepreneurs to start businesses.
paras.G: Individuals can also learn to treat failure differently. Psychologists describe a 'growth mindset', the belief that abilities can develop with effort, and suggest that people with this view recover more quickly from setbacks. The aim is not to enjoy failing but to ask, each time, what can be learned and what will be done differently next time.

paras.A: People have built dams for thousands of years to hold back water. The oldest known examples are in Jordan and Egypt, and ancient farmers in Mesopotamia and Central Asia used earth banks to direct floods onto their fields. Today, there are more than fifty thousand large dams in the world, and they play a major part in the supply of water and energy.
paras.B: The benefits are substantial. Reservoirs store water from wet seasons for use in dry ones, allowing farmers to irrigate crops and cities to maintain supplies. Dams control floods that once destroyed homes and harvests, and hydroelectric stations produce electricity without burning fuel. Around sixteen per cent of the world's electricity comes from this source, making it the largest renewable one.
paras.C: Some regions depend heavily on dams. In Central Asia, reservoirs in mountain countries store the snowmelt of spring and release it in summer, while the downstream countries use it for cotton, rice and wheat. Large projects such as the Aswan High Dam on the Nile gave Egypt protection against floods and droughts and a major source of electricity.
paras.D: However, dams have costs. Building a reservoir floods valleys, farmland, forests and sometimes towns. It is estimated that tens of millions of people have been moved from their homes by dam projects, often with little compensation. Historic sites may also be lost, and when the water rises, so does the grief of those who have to leave.
paras.E: The effects on rivers and wildlife are also profound. A dam interrupts the movement of fish such as salmon and sturgeon that migrate to spawn, and it traps sand and mud that would otherwise fertilise floodplains and build deltas. Downstream, rivers may carry less sediment, and coasts can erode. The flow of water, which once varied with the seasons, becomes artificial.
paras.F: Dams can also create tension between nations that share a river. Countries upstream want to store water or generate power, while those downstream fear shortages. Treaties and shared management, such as those on some rivers in Europe and Africa, can help, but where trust is low, projects can become matters of politics and even security.
paras.G: Recent trends are more cautious. Fewer large dams are being built in rich countries, and some old ones have been removed to restore rivers. Planners now consider alternatives such as solar power, better irrigation and smaller dams with ladders that fish can use. The challenge is to gain the benefits of stored water while limiting harm to people and nature.

paras.A: Over billions of years, nature has solved problems of strength, movement, energy and communication through the slow process of evolution. 'Biomimicry' is the practice of studying these solutions and applying them to human design. The term comes from Greek words meaning 'life' and 'imitation', but the idea is much older: Leonardo da Vinci studied birds when he sketched flying machines.
paras.B: A famous example is the Velcro fastener. In the 1940s, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral noticed seeds of burdock plants clinging to his dog's fur. Under a microscope, he saw tiny hooks that caught on loops of hair. He copied the principle with hooks and loops of nylon, and the invention is now used on everything from shoes to space suits.
paras.C: Transport has also drawn on nature. The front of a Japanese high-speed train was reshaped after engineers studied the kingfisher, a bird that dives into water with hardly a splash. The new design reduced noise when the train left tunnels at speed, and also saved energy. Wind turbine blades with bumps along the edge, modelled on the fins of humpback whales, can capture more energy in light breezes.
paras.D: In buildings, designers have looked at termite mounds. These towers, built by tiny insects, stay at a constant temperature despite changes outside, because of a network of tunnels that circulate air. An office building in Zimbabwe uses a similar principle to keep cool with little air conditioning, using a fraction of the energy of comparable structures.
paras.E: Materials science offers further examples. Spider silk is stronger than steel for its weight, and researchers are trying to produce similar fibres using bacteria. The leaves of the lotus plant repel water and dirt, inspiring self-cleaning paints and glass. The skin of sharks has a pattern that reduces the growth of bacteria, and it has been copied for use on hospital surfaces.
paras.F: What makes biomimicry attractive is that nature works within limits. Organisms use only local materials and energy, make no lasting waste and are shaped by constant testing. Designers who ask 'how would nature solve this?' may find answers that are efficient and sustainable, qualities that human industry needs urgently.
paras.G: Yet it is not a magic solution. Copying a shape without understanding its function can fail, and biological systems are very complex. The best results come when biologists, engineers and designers work together. If they succeed, the next great inventions may already exist in the living world, waiting for someone to look closely.

title: Clean Water and the Fight Against Disease

paras.A: Today, we turn on a tap and expect safe water to flow. In earlier centuries, this was not so. Diseases such as cholera and typhoid, spread through contaminated water, killed millions, and people had little idea why. The development of public sanitation, one of the quietest revolutions in history, has saved more lives than almost any medicine.
paras.B: A key moment came in London in 1854. During an outbreak of cholera, a doctor named John Snow plotted the homes of victims on a map and found that they were clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded officials to remove the handle of the pump, and the outbreak declined. His work led to the idea that cholera was carried by water rather than by 'bad air'.
paras.C: Governments responded by building sewers and water treatment systems. London's engineers created a large network of sewers in the 1860s, which carried waste away from the city, and many other cities followed. Filtering water through sand and treating it with chlorine, introduced early in the twentieth century, further reduced disease. Death rates in cities fell dramatically.
paras.D: Despite this progress, the problem has not been solved. According to the United Nations, around two billion people still lack access to safely managed drinking water, and more than three billion lack safe sanitation. Diarrhoea caused by unclean water remains a leading cause of death among young children, even though it is easily preventable.
paras.E: Solutions need not be complicated. Washing hands with soap can reduce diarrhoeal disease by around a third. Simple filters, boiling water and protecting wells from animals help families. Toilets that keep waste separate from water supplies are vital, and campaigns that have changed habits, as well as building toilets, have achieved lasting results.
paras.F: Larger systems demand money and planning. Pipes leak, pumps break and treatment plants require trained staff, so projects that are built without plans for maintenance often fail within a few years. Communities that take part in the design and manage the system themselves are more likely to keep it working.
paras.G: The benefits go beyond health. Children, especially girls, who spend hours carrying water cannot attend school, and clinics without clean water cannot treat patients safely. Providing safe water and sanitation is therefore one of the most cost-effective investments a country can make, with returns in health, education and economic growth. For this reason, the world's leaders have set a goal of safe water and sanitation for everybody, and progress, though uneven, shows that the goal can be reached.

paras.A: For a long time, scientists assumed that only humans could think, plan and use tools. Animals, it was believed, acted on instinct. Over the last fifty years, careful research has changed this view. We now know that many species show remarkable intelligence, though often in forms very different from our own.
paras.B: Tool use is the best-known example. In 1960, Jane Goodall observed chimpanzees in Tanzania stripping leaves from twigs and using them to extract termites from nests. Crows in New Caledonia make hooks from wire and branches, and in laboratory tests they solve puzzles in which they must use one tool to obtain another. Octopuses have been seen carrying coconut shells to use as shelter.
paras.C: Memory and planning have also been demonstrated. Some jays hide food in hundreds of places and remember where, and they even change their hiding places if they notice that they were watched by another bird. Elephants are said to remember the routes to water sources over long periods, and experienced females lead their herds through droughts.
paras.D: Communication can be sophisticated. Bees perform a 'waggle dance' that tells others the direction and distance of flowers. Dolphins use individual whistles that work like names, and vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for eagles, snakes and leopards, each causing a different response. Whether any of this is language in the human sense is still debated.
paras.E: Researchers use tests of self-awareness to compare species. In the mirror test, a mark is placed on an animal's body where it can see it only in a mirror; if the animal touches the mark on itself, it recognises its reflection. Great apes, dolphins, elephants and some magpies have passed, though critics note that the test favours animals that rely on sight.
paras.F: There are cautions. People have a tendency to see human thought in animal behaviour, and a clever result may sometimes be explained by simpler learning. Intelligence is also hard to compare: a dog's understanding of smell, or a bat's of sound, may be far greater than ours, but it is difficult for a human to test.
paras.G: These findings have moral importance. If animals can plan, feel and remember, then our treatment of them deserves serious thought, and many countries have strengthened laws on animal welfare. At the least, studying animal minds teaches humility about our own place in the natural world. Future research, using better tools and more patient observation, will probably reveal abilities that we have not yet imagined.

paras.A: The oceans cover seventy per cent of the Earth and hold most of its heat. Their water is always on the move, driven by wind, the rotation of the Earth and differences in temperature and saltiness. These movements, called ocean currents, carry warmth, nutrients and even floating seeds around the planet, and they have a major influence on climate.
paras.B: Surface currents are mostly driven by the wind. In each ocean, large circular systems called gyres turn clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the south. The Gulf Stream, a fast current in the North Atlantic, carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico towards Europe. Because of it, northwestern Europe is much milder than other regions at the same latitude, such as Labrador in Canada.
paras.C: Beneath the surface, there is a slower system known as the thermohaline circulation, from the Greek words for heat and salt. In polar regions, seawater becomes cold and salty as ice forms, so it becomes dense and sinks. This deep water then flows slowly along the ocean floor towards the equator, to rise again elsewhere after many centuries. The pattern is often called the 'global conveyor belt'.
paras.D: Currents influence life as well as weather. Where deep water rises to the surface, as it does off the coasts of Peru and Namibia, it brings nutrients that feed tiny plants called phytoplankton. These support huge numbers of fish, which is why such upwelling zones are among the richest fisheries in the world.
paras.E: Changes in the currents can have dramatic effects. Every few years, the winds over the tropical Pacific weaken and warm water spreads eastward, a pattern called El Niño. It disrupts fisheries off South America and alters weather around the globe, bringing floods to some regions and drought to others. A reverse pattern, La Niña, has opposite effects.
paras.F: Scientists are concerned about the effect of climate change. Melting ice adds fresh water to the North Atlantic, which could make the surface less dense and slow the sinking that drives the circulation. Measurements suggest the system may have weakened slightly in recent decades, though how much is uncertain. A major slowdown could make the climate of Europe colder, even as the planet warms.
paras.G: To observe such vast systems, researchers use floating robots, satellites and instruments on ships. More than three thousand robotic floats now drift through the oceans, diving to two kilometres and reporting temperature and saltiness. The data are helping to improve forecasts, and to reveal how the oceans shape the world's climate.

paras.A: Maps are among the oldest forms of human communication. The earliest known examples, scratched on clay or stone, date back thousands of years, and show fields, rivers and towns. From the beginning, maps have been more than records of places; they have been tools of trade, war and government, and expressions of how people understood their world.
paras.B: Ancient Greek scholars made major advances. Eratosthenes estimated the size of the Earth around 240 BC by comparing the length of shadows in two Egyptian cities, and his result was remarkably close to the modern figure. Ptolemy, in the second century AD, described how to locate places by lines of latitude and longitude, a system still in use.
paras.C: In the medieval Islamic world, geographers combined knowledge from traders and travellers with the Greek tradition. Al-Idrisi, working in Sicily in the twelfth century, produced a detailed map of the known world for King Roger II. It was drawn with south at the top, a reminder that the convention of north at the top is not natural but cultural.
paras.D: The age of exploration changed mapmaking. European sailors needed charts for oceans, and the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator devised in 1569 a projection in which lines of constant compass direction appear straight, which was valuable for navigators. However, it greatly enlarges regions near the poles, so that Greenland appears as large as Africa, though Africa is about fourteen times bigger.
paras.E: All flat maps distort, since a sphere cannot be flattened without stretching or cutting it. Mapmakers must therefore choose which properties to preserve, such as area, shape or distance, and projections serve different purposes. The choice may also carry meaning: a map that places one's own country in the centre can suggest its importance.
paras.F: In recent decades, satellites and computers have transformed cartography. Global positioning systems, which measure signals from satellites, allow anyone with a phone to find their position within a few metres. Digital maps are updated constantly with information from users, and layers of data, from traffic to disease, can be added and compared within seconds.
paras.G: Even so, human judgement remains essential. Someone must decide what to show, what to name and where borders lie, and those decisions can be sensitive. Modern mapmakers also work with communities to record places that official maps ignore, such as informal settlements. A map, after all, is never the territory itself, but always a point of view. Reading a map critically, by asking who made it and why, is therefore a skill worth teaching to every student.

paras.A: Most of what we believe, we have not checked for ourselves. We have never measured the distance to the sun, tested the safety of a vaccine or examined the structure of a bridge before crossing it. We rely on experts, people with training and experience, to tell us what is true and what is safe. Without such trust, modern life would be impossible.
paras.B: Trust is reasonable when experts are competent, honest and answerable for their work. Scientific institutions try to deserve it by publishing methods, allowing others to repeat results and correcting mistakes openly. The process of peer review, in which independent specialists examine a study before it is published, is meant to catch errors, though it is far from perfect.
paras.C: Expertise, however, is narrow. A brilliant physicist is not necessarily a good judge of nutrition, and an economist may know little about medicine. Problems arise when specialists speak confidently outside their field, or when media present a single voice as 'the expert' on matters far beyond that person's knowledge.
paras.D: Experts also make mistakes, and some have misled the public. Examples such as advice about diet that later changed, or the failure to predict a financial crisis, remind us that knowledge develops. Critics argue that experts sometimes ignore ordinary people's practical experience, and that their judgement can be influenced by money or by the wish to protect a reputation.
paras.E: In recent years, surveys in many countries have recorded a decline in trust. Some of this is understandable, but some arises from deliberate campaigns that spread doubt for political or commercial gain. The internet has also allowed anyone to publish, so that the voice of a trained specialist may appear next to the voice of someone with no knowledge at all.
paras.F: How, then, can a non-expert judge whom to trust? Researchers suggest practical questions. Does the person have relevant training, and do other experts in the field agree? Who pays for the research, and might they gain from a particular result? Is the claim supported by evidence that can be checked, or does it rely on a single story? A confident tone is not evidence.
paras.G: Healthy societies need both trust and questioning. Blind acceptance leaves people open to error, while automatic suspicion makes cooperation impossible. The aim is a calibrated trust, which gives weight to reliable sources, and remains open to being corrected. Experts, in turn, can help by explaining their reasoning and admitting uncertainty plainly. In the end, trust is something that must be earned again and again, by both individuals and institutions.

paras.A: It is natural to think that creativity needs freedom. Give a person unlimited time, money and choice, and surely something wonderful will appear. Yet many artists, writers and designers report the opposite: that limits help them to think. A blank page can be frightening, while a clear challenge gives the mind something to push against.
paras.B: Examples are easy to find. Poets have for centuries written in strict forms such as the sonnet, with fourteen lines and fixed rhymes, and produced some of their finest work. Jazz musicians improvise inside a set of chords, and the architect who must fit a building onto a narrow plot may find a more interesting solution than one who has an open field.
paras.C: Psychologists have tried to explain the effect. Constraints reduce the number of options, and so cut the time spent worrying about choices. They also force people to leave the obvious path. If the usual way is not allowed, a person must search for another, and in doing so may find something new. In experiments, groups given limited materials sometimes produced more original ideas than groups given plentiful ones.
paras.D: Technology provides a modern example. The first mobile phones allowed only 160 characters in a text message, and users invented abbreviations and new styles of writing to fit the limit. Early video games had tiny memories, so designers learned to create memorable characters with a few pixels and simple sounds, some of which are still popular decades later.
paras.E: Not all constraints are equally helpful, however. Limits that are too severe, or that seem arbitrary and unfair, can discourage. Research suggests that the best constraints are those that a person understands and accepts, or has chosen. A deadline can focus effort, but constant pressure with no time for reflection tends to reduce creativity.
paras.F: Organisations can use this knowledge. Some companies run short projects with fixed budgets and time, and ask teams to solve problems with only a few resources. Teachers sometimes set tasks such as writing a story in exactly fifty words, which encourages students to consider each word. A good limit works like a frame around a picture.
paras.G: Freedom still matters. People need time to explore, to play and to be bored, and ideas often come when the mind is relaxed. The best conditions may be a mixture: wide freedom to choose a direction, together with a sharp limit that makes the work interesting. Creativity grows where space and structure meet. Teachers and managers who understand this can set tasks that are open enough to inspire and tight enough to guide.

paras.A: Elite athletes seem to perform feats beyond ordinary people, and part of the reason is natural talent. But increasingly, sport is also a science. Researchers in physiology, psychology, nutrition and engineering study every aspect of training and competition in search of small improvements that may decide the result of a race by hundredths of a second.
paras.B: Training has changed greatly. Coaches once relied on instinct and tradition, but today, athletes wear devices that measure heart rate, speed and movement, and software analyses the data to show how hard to push and when to rest. Research has shown that recovery is as important as exercise itself, since the body adapts to stress during rest, not during the effort.
paras.C: Nutrition has also become more precise. Endurance athletes carefully plan how much carbohydrate to eat before and during events, because the body's stores of this fuel run out after about ninety minutes of intense effort. Hydration is monitored, too, as losing even two per cent of body weight in sweat can reduce performance, while drinking far too much can be dangerous.
paras.D: Equipment is shaped by engineering. Swimmers' suits, running shoes with springy foam and carbon plates, and bicycles tested in wind tunnels have all helped to push records. Some innovations were so effective that officials introduced rules to limit them, in order that competitions measure the athlete rather than the technology.
paras.E: The mind matters as much as the body. Sports psychologists teach techniques such as setting goals, imagining a performance in detail and controlling attention under pressure. A famous finding is that experts can 'choke' when they think too much about movements that should be automatic, which is why coaches train athletes to focus on their goal rather than on each part of the action.
paras.F: There are ethical limits. Drugs and other methods to improve performance are banned, and testing laboratories use sophisticated methods to detect them. The temptation can be strong, since the rewards of success are great. Some experts argue that technology and genetic advantages, too, raise questions about fairness that sport has not yet settled.
paras.G: For ordinary people, the lessons are practical. Regular exercise with adequate rest, balanced meals, enough sleep and a positive attitude benefit health at any level. Elite sport may seem remote, but the knowledge it creates often finds its way into schools, gyms and clinics, and helps all of us to move better and to enjoy it more. The next advance may come from a laboratory, but it may equally come from a coach who notices something nobody else has seen.

paras.A: Many people feel they never have enough time, and a large industry of books, apps and courses promises to help. Yet some of the advice is based on myths. Researchers who study how people really use their time have found that the popular picture of the highly organised person, who plans every minute, is often misleading.
paras.B: One myth is that multitasking makes us more productive. In fact, the brain cannot do two demanding tasks at once; it switches rapidly between them, losing time and accuracy at every change. Experiments show that people who answer messages while working take longer to finish and make more errors. The feeling of being busy is not the same as getting things done.
paras.C: Another myth is that the answer to overload is a longer to-do list. A list of fifty items does not make time for any of them. Experts recommend instead choosing a few priorities each day, the tasks that matter most, and doing them first, when energy is high. The rest can be postponed or dropped, and acknowledging that not everything will be done reduces stress.
paras.D: A third myth is that working longer hours always yields more. Studies of factory workers and office staff show that output per hour falls as the day lengthens, and that very long weeks may produce little more than normal ones. Rest, sleep and breaks restore attention, so that people who stop on time often accomplish as much as those who work late.
paras.E: Some people believe that procrastination is simply laziness. Psychologists see it more as a way of avoiding unpleasant feelings, such as fear of failure or boredom with a task. Strategies that reduce the discomfort, such as breaking the job into small steps and starting for just five minutes, are often more effective than blaming oneself.
paras.F: Time management is also more than personal technique. A person with a rigid employer, unpredictable shifts or caring duties cannot simply 'organise better'. Some of the stress felt by workers comes from the way work is arranged, and changes such as flexible schedules or reduced meetings can do more than any app.
paras.G: The most useful advice is therefore modest. Decide what is important, protect time for it, accept limits and take breaks. Time cannot be created or saved, only spent. The question is whether we spend it on what we value, which is a question that no schedule can answer for us. Perhaps the real goal is not to do more, but to leave room for the things that make a day worthwhile.
